title: They begged the Son of God… not to send them away.
paragraphs: They begged the Son of God… not to send them away.
Not humans.
Demons.
That detail should disturb you more than most people realize.
Because when hell speaks to Jesus, it reveals things religious performances never could.

The screaming man in the tombs was not just a horror story.
He was somebody’s son.
Somebody’s memory.
Somebody who once laughed at a table before chains replaced conversations.

And the terrifying part is…
Scripture says nobody could bind him anymore.

Not with chains.
Not with religion.
Not with force.
Not with human effort.
Because spiritual bondage always becomes stronger than human solutions.
In Gospel of Mark 5:1–20, Jesus steps onto the shores of the Decapolis region, and immediately a demonized man runs toward Him from the tombs.
The Greek text says:

“καὶ κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ”
(kai kraxas phōnē megalē)
“and crying out with a great voice.”

This was not calm.
Not theatrical.
Not symbolic.
This was torment screaming in the presence of holiness.
And then something shocking happens.
The demons recognize Jesus instantly.

Before many people in Israel understood who Christ truly was…
demons already knew.
They say:

“Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί, Ἰησοῦ, υἱὲ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου;”
(Ti emoi kai soi, Iēsou, huie tou Theou tou Hypsistou?)
“What have You to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?”
Demons do not struggle with atheism.
They know exactly who Jesus is.
And that should terrify every lukewarm soul who thinks mere intellectual belief saves them.
Because according to Epistle of James 2:19:
“Even the demons believe—and tremble.”
The Greek word for tremble is:

“φρίσσουσιν”
(phrissousin)

It means:
to shudder,
to bristle in terror,
to quake violently.

Demons have better theology than many churchgoers.
But they do not have surrender.
That is the difference between information and salvation.
And then comes the question that opens a terrifying spiritual window:
“Do not send us away.”
Why?
Why would demons beg?
Why would beings that torment humans suddenly sound afraid?
Because they understood something many humans still ignore:
Jesus has absolute authority over the unseen realm.

Not partial authority.
Not symbolic authority.
Total authority.
The demons knew judgment was coming.
In Gospel of Luke 8:31, the text says:

“καὶ παρεκάλουν αὐτὸν ἵνα μὴ ἐπιτάξῃ αὐτοῖς εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον ἀπελθεῖν.”
(kai parekaloun auton hina mē epitaxē autois eis tēn abysson apelthein)
“And they begged Him not to command them to depart into the Abyss.”

The word “ἄβυσσος” (abyssos) means:
the abyss,
the bottomless place,
the prison-like deep.

This was not mythology.
This was spiritual reality.
The demons were terrified of being confined before their appointed judgment.
They knew Jesus was not merely a teacher.
He was Judge.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because most people only read this passage as a supernatural event.

But if you slow down…
you realize this man represents millions of people alive today.
People smiling online while dying internally.
People living among emotional tombs.
People cutting themselves with hidden shame.

People isolated.
Addicted.
Tormented.
Numb.
Exhausted.
The text says the man cried night and day among the tombs.
Night and day.
Pain without pause.
Some of you reading this understand that sentence too well.

You know what it feels like when torment follows you into the night.
When your mind becomes loud in the dark.
When shame feels stronger than hope.
And this is why this encounter matters so much:
Jesus crossed an entire sea for one broken man.
One.

Not a crowd.
Not a stadium.
Not a religious conference.
One tormented soul.
Do you understand how offensive that is to performance-driven religion?
Christ will interrupt entire regions for one suffering person.
The demons begged Jesus not to send them away because darkness cannot survive unrestricted holiness.

Light does not negotiate with darkness.
Truth does not compromise with lies.
Christ does not coexist with demonic ownership.
And then comes another haunting detail.
Jesus asks:
“What is your name?”
The response:
“My name is Legion, for we are many.”
The Greek word “Λεγιὼν” (Legiōn) refers to a Roman military unit often containing thousands of soldiers.

This man was not merely oppressed.
He was overwhelmed.
Occupied.
Invaded internally.
And yet Jesus was never intimidated.
Not once.

No panic.
No ritual struggle.
No incantation.
Just authority.

Because the kingdom of darkness is loud…
but never sovereign.
Please hear this carefully:

The power was never in volume.
The power was always in Christ.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to remember tonight.

Your fear is loud.
Your trauma is loud.
Your addiction is loud.
Your depression is loud.
But none of those things are king.
Jesus is.
The demons begged because they understood what humanity often refuses to accept:
When Christ arrives, ownership changes.
And after Jesus casts them out, the townspeople find the man sitting peacefully, clothed, and in his right mind.
Think about that.

The man society gave up on…
restored.

The man chains could not fix…
healed.

The man isolation buried…
redeemed.
This is why the Gospel is not self-help.

Self-help says:
manage yourself.

Jesus says:
be made new.
And what happens next may be the saddest moment in the entire story.
The townspeople ask Jesus to leave.
Imagine that.

A region witnessed undeniable deliverance…
and still preferred comfort over Christ.
Because sometimes people become more afraid of holy disruption than demonic bondage.
Some people would rather keep familiar darkness than surrender to transforming light.
And that still happens today.

Jesus delivers someone from addiction…
and old friends disappear.

Jesus changes somebody’s heart…
and suddenly they no longer fit into environments built on sin.
Freedom exposes darkness.
Transformation makes people uncomfortable.
But the restored man begs to follow Jesus.
And Jesus tells him to stay and testify.
Why?
Because healed people become evidence.

Your scars become sermons.
Your survival becomes proof.
Your restoration becomes warfare against hopelessness.
Somebody reading this has been ashamed of their testimony for too long.
But heaven does not waste redeemed pain.

The enemy wanted the man isolated in tombs.
Jesus restored him to purpose.
And maybe that is why this story grips the soul so deeply.
Because every human being is eventually forced to answer one terrifying question:
Who truly has authority over my life?
The demons already knew the answer.
Do you?
Some of you have been surviving spiritually while pretending to be alive emotionally.

Jesus did not cross the sea to condemn the broken man.
He crossed it to free him.
Send this to someone battling darkness internally.
And follow for daily biblical truth, healing, conviction, spiritual warfare understanding, discipleship, and encouragement rooted completely in Jesus Christ.
One encounter with Jesus can undo years of darkness that everybody else thought was permanent.
